title: The Endless Chip War
gist: Interview with semiconductor expert Rakesh Kumar: chip wars are old, TSMC and Samsung will likely exit legacy chips within 2-3 years, innovation is slowing, NVIDIA is the AI 'pick and shovel' winner whose CUDA moat will weaken, and the US should friendshore minerals, back alternative lithography and prop up Intel Foundry.

insights.claim: Chip wars, shortages, tariffs and export controls are not new: the US used trade and geopolitical pressure in the mid-1980s to kill Japanese chip competition, and denial of chips helped cripple Soviet precision-guided weapons.
insights.speaker: Rakesh Kumar
insights.so_what: Current US-China chip controls follow a long precedent of weaponized chip access.
insights.locator: It is worth clarifying that chip wars

insights.claim: Roughly two-thirds of chips use technology commercialized before 2005, and the author expects foundries such as TSMC and Samsung to exit legacy chip manufacturing within two to three years, with Singapore filling the vacuum and India struggling with scale.
insights.speaker: Rakesh Kumar
insights.so_what: Legacy-node supply may tighten and reprice; watch Singapore and Chinese legacy capacity.

insights.claim: Replacing legacy chips is hard: costs pass down the supply chain, recertification is needed in aerospace, medical and automotive, and legacy chips withstand harsh conditions better for some defense uses.
insights.speaker: Rakesh Kumar
insights.so_what: Legacy chip scarcity can hit autos and defense disproportionately.

insights.claim: Microprocessor speed now rises only 10-15 percent a year, AI chip computation falls behind AI model demand by a further 200 times every two years, and GPUs use hundreds of millions of times more energy than the brain for equivalent computation.
insights.speaker: Rakesh Kumar
insights.so_what: Supports the thesis that efficiency gains are slowing, favoring power, cooling and novel-architecture bets.

insights.claim: The US should set up three to four time-bound industry-government consortia on alternative computing, novel devices, novel materials and fabrication, and make participation a condition of federal chip funding, as an earlier 1997 consortium led to EUV lithography in 2001.
insights.speaker: Rakesh Kumar
insights.so_what: Policy direction that could redirect CHIPS funds toward R&D consortia.

insights.claim: NVIDIA, like Intel in the PC era, captures a large share of AI industry profits as the 'pick and shovel' provider while model and application companies compete for leftovers; power, cooling, networking and chipmaking equipment firms will join them.
insights.speaker: Rakesh Kumar
insights.so_what: Infrastructure suppliers retain the economics ahead of model makers.

insights.claim: Developers' reluctance to leave NVIDIA's CUDA platform is a software moat comparable to Intel's, but as AI gets better at writing and porting code the moat will weaken.
insights.speaker: Rakesh Kumar
insights.so_what: CUDA lock-in erodes as AI-assisted code porting improves, which is a medium-term risk to NVIDIA's pricing power.

insights.claim: The author expects China, and eventually Europe, India, South Korea and Singapore seeking sovereign AI, to reach near parity in all but the most advanced AI capabilities, as China did in all but the most advanced chips.
insights.speaker: Rakesh Kumar
insights.so_what: Export controls delay but may not prevent near-parity outside the frontier.
insights.locator: Fourth, chips became a geopolitical lever

insights.claim: Because the Pentagon is a tiny fraction of chip demand and authorized-source and chain-of-custody mandates are abandoned in conflict and shortages, the author recommends physical and electrical verification of defense chips (imaging, decapsulation, fingerprinting) and built-in authentication features.
insights.speaker: Rakesh Kumar
insights.so_what: Chip testing and authentication vendors are potential beneficiaries of defense demand.
insights.locator: The key challenge is that the Pentagon

insights.claim: The US should friendshore critical minerals rather than compete directly with China on refining, and pursue next-generation lithography such as nanoimprint and x-ray rather than replicating ASML's EUV, which took three decades and tens or hundreds of billions of dollars.
insights.speaker: Rakesh Kumar
insights.so_what: ASML's EUV position is seen as near-unreplicable; leapfrog bets are speculative.
insights.locator: As China found out over the last decade

insights.claim: To fix single-company manufacturing dominance, the author would steer NVIDIA, Apple and Qualcomm to manufacture at Intel and have Amazon, Microsoft and Google buy Intel-made chips, with federal funds for equity or chips, until Intel's advanced manufacturing is self-sustaining.
insights.speaker: Rakesh Kumar
insights.so_what: Supports a policy-backed anchor-customer path for Intel Foundry; Intel can now make chips as advanced as TSMC's according to the author.
